blocks.h: 1. What Article 16 does, and why one convention needs several routes

blocks.p: Article 16 is the amendment machinery of MARPOL. Paragraph 16(1) sets the frame: the Convention may be amended by any of the procedures specified in the article. There are two routes to adoption - after consideration by the Organization (16(2)) and by a Conference of Parties (16(3)) - and, within them, the acceptance mechanism differs according to which part of the Convention is being amended. That is the flexibility the question refers to: the articles are framework and are amended slowly, by express consent; the Annexes and their appendices carry technical detail and are amended quickly, by default.

blocks.h: 2. The steps common to every amendment considered by the Organization

ul: Proposal and circulation (16(2)(a)) - any Party may propose an amendment. It goes to the Organization, and the Secretary-General circulates it to all Members of the Organization and all Parties at least six months before it is considered.
Reference to an appropriate body (16(2)(b)) - in practice the Marine Environment Protection Committee.
Participation (16(2)(c)) - Parties to the Convention are entitled to take part whether or not they are Members of the Organization.
Adoption (16(2)(d)) - by a two-thirds majority of only the Parties present and voting. Members of the Organization that are not Parties do not vote.

Communication for acceptance (16(2)(e)) - the Secretary-General sends the adopted text to all Parties. Adoption is not entry into force; acceptance is the step that follows, and it is here that the routes diverge.

blocks.p: Under 16(2)(f)(i) an amendment to an article of the Convention is deemed accepted only on the date it is accepted by two thirds of the Parties, the combined merchant fleets of which constitute not less than 50 per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant fleet. Both conditions must be satisfied - a count of States and a tonnage share. Nothing is presumed: a State that says nothing has not accepted. Protocol II (arbitration) follows this same procedure by 16(2)(f)(v), and by 16(5) so does the adoption of an entirely new Annex. This is deliberately demanding, because these provisions define the obligations themselves.

blocks.h: 4. Amending an Annex - tacit acceptance by default

blocks.p: 16(2)(f)(ii) is the provision that makes MARPOL efficient. An amendment to an Annex is deemed accepted in accordance with the procedure in (f)(iii) - the tacit procedure - unless the appropriate body, at the time of adoption, determines that the explicit (f)(i) test shall apply instead. Tacit acceptance is therefore the default for the technical Annexes, and explicit acceptance the exception the Committee must positively choose.

The reservation attached to it is examinable. At any time before an Annex amendment enters into force, a Party may notify the Secretary-General that its express approval is necessary before the amendment binds it, and the Secretary-General notifies the other Parties of that notification and its date. Protocol I (reports on incidents involving harmful substances) follows the Annex procedures by 16(2)(f)(iv).

blocks.h: 5. Amending an Appendix to an Annex - the tacit mechanism itself

blocks.p: The tacit procedure is drafted in 16(2)(f)(iii), where it applies directly to an appendix to an Annex - the certificate forms, lists and schedules. The amendment is deemed accepted at the end of a period fixed by the appropriate body at adoption, which shall be not less than ten months, unless within that period an objection is communicated to the Organization by not less than one third of the Parties, or by Parties whose combined merchant fleets constitute not less than 50 per cent of world gross tonnage, whichever condition is fulfilled.

Note the contrast with limb 3, and make it explicitly. The acceptance test for an article is conjunctive - two thirds of Parties and 50 per cent of tonnage. The objection test here is disjunctive - one third of Parties or 50 per cent of tonnage, whichever is met first. Silence accepts; only a sufficiently weighty objection defeats.

blocks.h: 6. Amendment by a Conference of Parties

blocks.p: Under 16(3), on the request of a Party concurred in by at least one third of the Parties, the Organization shall convene a Conference of Parties to consider amendments. A Conference adopts by a two-thirds majority of the Parties present and voting, and the Secretary-General communicates the amendment to all Contracting Parties for acceptance. Unless the Conference decides otherwise, acceptance and entry into force then follow 16(2)(f) and (g) - so the Conference route changes the forum, not the acceptance mechanism. This route produced the 1978 Protocol; it is available but rarely used, because the Committee route is faster.

blocks.h: 7. Entry into force, and the limits on any amendment

ul: 16(2)(g)(i) - for an article, Protocol II, or an Annex or Protocol I not under the tacit route, the amendment enters into force six months after acceptance, and binds only those Parties which declared that they accept it.

16(2)(g)(ii) - under the tacit route the amendment enters into force six months after acceptance for all Parties, except those which had declared that they do not accept it or had made the express-approval declaration under (f)(ii). This is the whole practical difference: silence binds you.

16(4) - for an Optional Annex (III, IV, V and VI), 'Party to the Convention' means a Party bound by that Annex; and a Party declining an Annex amendment is treated as a non-Party only for the purpose of that amendment.

16(6) - unless expressly provided otherwise, an amendment relating to the structure of a ship applies only to ships for which the building contract is placed, or the keel laid in the absence of a contract, on or after the date the amendment comes into force. Existing ships are not required to be rebuilt.

16(7) - an amendment to a Protocol or an Annex must relate to the substance of that Protocol or Annex and be consistent with the articles. The technical fast track cannot be used to change the framework.

blocks.p: The question hands you its own structure - 'depending on what part of MARPOL is being amended' - and the marks follow it. An answer organised as article / Annex / appendix / Conference is answering the question asked. An answer that simply describes tacit acceptance for three pages is answering a different, easier one. Give the common procedural steps once (16(2)(a)-(e)), then take each part of the Convention in turn, then close on entry into force. The single most valuable paragraph is the contrast between the conjunctive acceptance test for articles and the disjunctive objection test for the tacit route.

blocks.h: The idea behind the two-speed design

blocks.p: MARPOL is called flexible because it is deliberately built at two speeds. The articles carry the bargain the States struck - scope, jurisdiction, enforcement, dispute settlement. Changing that bargain needs express consent, so it is slow and it binds only those who say yes. The Annexes and appendices carry engineering: oil discharge limits, tank arrangements, sulphur limits, survey and certificate forms. If those needed express ratification by two thirds of States every time, MARPOL would be permanently a decade behind the fleet. So the drafters inverted the default for the technical layer: adoption plus silence equals acceptance. 16(7) is the safeguard that keeps the fast track honest - a technical amendment must stay consistent with the articles, so the quick procedure cannot be used to rewrite the slow one.

Candidates lose marks by blurring three different numbers. Adoption is a two-thirds majority of the Parties present and voting (16(2)(d)) - a meeting-room vote. Acceptance of an article amendment needs two thirds of the Parties whose combined fleets are not less than 50 per cent of world gross tonnage (16(2)(f)(i)) - two conditions, both required. Defeating a tacit amendment needs objection by one third of the Parties or Parties holding not less than 50 per cent of world gross tonnage, whichever is fulfilled (16(2)(f)(iii)) - either will do. And the tacit period is not less than ten months, fixed at adoption; with the further six months to entry into force under 16(2)(g)(ii), sixteen months is the practical floor, which is why amendments are commonly seen entering into force roughly eighteen months to two years after adoption.

ul: Saying MARPOL 'is amended by tacit acceptance' and stopping. That is true of the Annexes and appendices and false of the articles, and the question expressly asks you to distinguish by part.
Confusing adoption with entry into force. Adoption is a vote; acceptance is a separate stage; entry into force is six months later again.
Giving the objection threshold as 'two thirds'. Objection is one third of Parties, or the 50 per cent tonnage limb.
Treating the two limbs of the article test as alternatives. 16(2)(f)(i) requires two thirds of Parties and that those Parties hold at least 50 per cent of world tonnage.
Forgetting that a Party can opt out of tacit acceptance in advance under 16(2)(f)(ii) by requiring its express approval.
Omitting the Conference route in 16(3) altogether - the question says 'multiple ways', and there are two routes to adoption, not one.
Asserting that a new Annex is added by tacit acceptance. 16(5) puts a new annex on the article procedure.

blocks.p:
'A sulphur limit amendment was adopted last October. Does it bind India automatically?' If it is an Annex VI amendment adopted under the tacit route, then yes - unless India objected within the period fixed at adoption, or had previously notified that its express approval is necessary. Silence binds.

'Could MEPC use tacit acceptance to change Article 4 on violations?' No. Article amendments run under 16(2)(f)(i), and 16(7) requires an Annex or Protocol amendment to relate to the substance of that Annex or Protocol and to be consistent with the articles.

'A new double-hull requirement is adopted this year - does your existing ship have to be rebuilt?' Not by force of Article 16. Under 16(6), unless expressly provided otherwise, an amendment relating to the structure of a ship applies only to ships contracted, or keel-laid in the absence of a contract, on or after the date it comes into force. Note the qualifier: MARPOL amendments frequently do expressly provide otherwise, so check the amendment.

ul: How long before consideration must a proposed amendment be circulated? At least six months (16(2)(a)).
Who may vote on adoption? Only the Parties to the Convention present and voting, by a two-thirds majority - whether or not they are Members of the Organization.
What is the minimum tacit acceptance period? Not less than ten months, fixed by the appropriate body at adoption.
How is a tacit amendment defeated? Objection by not less than one third of the Parties, or by Parties holding not less than 50 per cent of world gross tonnage.
How long after acceptance does an amendment enter into force? Six months.
Which procedure applies to Protocol I and Protocol II? Protocol I follows the Annexes; Protocol II follows the articles.
How is a wholly new Annex adopted? By the article procedure, under 16(5).
What does Article 16(4) do for Optional Annexes? 'Party to the Convention' is read as a Party bound by that Annex, and a Party declining an amendment is a non-Party only for that amendment.

blocks.p: Two routes, three targets, two clocks. The two routes to adoption are the Organization (16(2)) and a Conference (16(3)). The three targets are the article, the Annex and the appendix - slow, fast-by-default, fast. The two clocks are the tacit period of not less than ten months and the six months from acceptance to entry into force. For the thresholds: AND for articles, OR against annexes - two thirds of Parties and half the tonnage to accept an article; one third of Parties or half the tonnage to object to a tacit amendment.

questions.understand_first: The thing to hold onto is that MARPOL deliberately runs at two speeds, and Article 16 is where the gearbox lives. The articles are the political bargain between States, so they change only when States expressly say yes. The Annexes are engineering - discharge limits, tank arrangements, certificate forms - and if those needed express ratification every time, the Convention would never keep up with the fleet. So for the technical layer the drafters reversed the default: once an amendment is adopted, saying nothing means accepting it. Everything else in the article - the thresholds, the ten months, the opt-out - is detail around that one inversion.
questions.memory_cue: TWO routes - the Organization and a Conference (1, 6). THREE targets - article, Annex, appendix (3, 4, 5). TWO clocks - ten months and six months (5, 7).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the MARPOL amendment question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What Article 16 does and why several routes. 2 Common steps under the Organization. 3 Articles - explicit. 4 Annexes - tacit by default. 5 Appendices - the tacit mechanism. 6 Conference of Parties. 7 Entry into force and limits.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 3 to 5 are the part-by-part answer the question expressly asks for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which parts of MARPOL are amended by explicit acceptance, and which by tacit?
retrieval_cards.answer: Explicit: the articles, Protocol II, and a wholly new Annex (16(2)(f)(i), (f)(v), 16(5)). Tacit by default: the Annexes, their appendices and Protocol I (16(2)(f)(ii), (iii), (iv)).
retrieval_cards.why: The question asks you to distinguish by part - this is the spine of the answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the acceptance threshold for an amendment to an ARTICLE of MARPOL?
retrieval_cards.answer: Acceptance by two thirds of the Parties, the combined merchant fleets of which constitute not less than 50 per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant fleet. Both conditions must be met.
retrieval_cards.why: Conjunctive - candidates routinely give it as one or the other.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is a tacit amendment to a MARPOL Annex or appendix defeated?
retrieval_cards.answer: By an objection communicated within the period fixed at adoption - not less than ten months - by not less than one third of the Parties, OR by Parties whose combined fleets are not less than 50 per cent of world gross tonnage, whichever condition is fulfilled.
retrieval_cards.why: Disjunctive, and the threshold is one third, not two thirds.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does an adopted tacit amendment bind a Party that said nothing?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes. Under 16(2)(g)(ii) it enters into force six months after acceptance for all Parties except those which declared they do not accept it, or which had notified under 16(2)(f)(ii) that their express approval is necessary.
retrieval_cards.why: Silence accepts - the whole practical point of the tacit route.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is a MARPOL amendment adopted by a Conference of Parties?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under 16(3), on the request of a Party concurred in by at least one third of the Parties, the Organization convenes a Conference. It adopts by a two-thirds majority of Parties present and voting, and unless it decides otherwise, acceptance and entry into force follow 16(2)(f) and (g).
retrieval_cards.why: The second route to adoption - omitted by most answers.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which provision stops the technical fast track being used to change the framework?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 16(7) - an amendment to a Protocol or Annex must relate to the substance of that Protocol or Annex and be consistent with the articles of the Convention.
retrieval_cards.why: The safeguard that makes the two-speed design legitimate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does a new MARPOL structural requirement apply to ships already in service?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under 16(6), unless expressly provided otherwise, an amendment relating to the structure of a ship applies only to ships for which the building contract is placed, or the keel laid in the absence of a contract, on or after the date it comes into force. Amendments often do provide otherwise, so read the amendment.
retrieval_cards.why: The default is non-retroactive, but the qualifier is load-bearing and is often dropped.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How long must a proposed amendment be circulated before it is considered?
retrieval_cards.answer: At least six months, by the Secretary-General, to all Members of the Organization and all Parties to the Convention - Article 16(2)(a).
retrieval_cards.why: Distinct from the six months between acceptance and entry into force.

blocks.h: 1. a) What FSA is, and who it is for

blocks.p: Formal Safety Assessment is set out in MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.12/Rev.2, Revised Guidelines for Formal Safety Assessment (FSA) for use in the IMO rule-making process, of 9 April 2018. The title states its purpose: a structured, auditable methodology by which the Organization decides whether, and how, to regulate a hazard, balancing safety benefit against cost. It is not a shipboard risk assessment or a permit-to-work system. The question is therefore how a proportionate rule for this cargo was, and is being, arrived at.

blocks.h: 2. Step 1 - identifying the hazards of this cargo

ul: Thermal runaway - an exothermic internal reaction that becomes self-sustaining and generates its own oxidant, so it cannot be smothered and continues without external air;
propagation cell to cell and module to module, and thence vehicle to vehicle in a close stow;
initiators - internal cell defects, mechanical damage in handling or lashing, over-charge, high state of charge on shipment, charging on board;
vent gas - flammable and toxic, able to accumulate in an enclosed vehicle space and produce a gas explosion rather than a simple fire;
re-ignition hours or days after apparent extinction, defeating a normal fire-out judgement;

mis-declaration and concealment - cells as cargo may be undeclared or wrongly classified, and a battery electric vehicle is not a labelled package at all, so the energy is invisible to the stowage plan.

blocks.h: 3. Step 2 - assessing the risk on a ro-ro deck

blocks.p: Risk is frequency times consequence, estimated from casualty returns, incident and near-miss data, cell testing and fire modelling - with the Rev.2 requirement that the reliability, uncertainty and validity of that data be assessed and reported rather than assumed.

ul: Frequency is low per vehicle but rising with fleet electrification, and exposure is concentrated - one deck may hold thousands of units;

consequence escalates because a ro-ro space is a large undivided volume, vehicles stowed centimetres apart, with no cargo-hold fire divisions and ramps and ventilation trunks carrying heat and smoke between decks;
on a ro-pax the dominant risk is to life; on a pure car and truck carrier it is total loss of the ship, and a series of well-known casualties supplied the evidence;
manual firefighting on a loaded deck is near impossible, so the model must assume fixed systems and boundaries are what will actually be available.

blocks.h: 4. Steps 3 and 4 - risk control options and whether they pay

blocks.p: Risk control options are generated and grouped, then tested by cost-benefit assessment using indices such as the cost of averting a fatality, so a measure is recommended only where the safety gain justifies the cost across the world fleet:

ul: detection - earlier, better-located, individually identifiable so the seat of fire is known, with combined smoke and heat sensing;
suppression - drencher and water-based systems of adequate coverage and capacity, aligned with detection sections so the right section operates;
containment - insulated boundaries, ventilation shut-down and control of openings;
operational and design - state-of-charge limits on shipment, segregation and dedicated stowage, restrictions on charging at sea, video monitoring, crew procedures;
options are ranked, and those effective but disproportionately costly are rejected transparently - which is why the outcome is a specific set of measures rather than everything technically possible.

blocks.h: 5. Step 5 - what the recommendations actually became

blocks.p: The risk-based work on ro-ro fire safety - notably the EMSA FIRESAFE I and FIRESAFE II studies of fire dynamics, system performance and operational factors - entered the regulatory system in two stages:

ul: MSC.1/Circ.1615, Interim Guidelines for Minimizing the Incidence and Consequences of Fires in Ro-Ro Spaces and Special Category Spaces, carried key outcomes into guidance while mandatory work continued;

resolution MSC.550(108) then amended SOLAS chapter II-2 regulations 7 and 20 and MSC.555(108) amended FSS Code chapters 7 and 9, both adopted at MSC 108 in May 2024 and in force on 1 January 2026 - that is, on 1 January of the year in which this paper was sat;

requirements include individually identifiable fixed detection with combined smoke and heat detectors, detection aligned with deluge sections, detection on weather decks used for vehicles, an effective video monitoring system with at least seven days of replay at a continuously manned control station, and A-60 boundaries on passenger ships carrying more than 36 passengers;
they apply to ships constructed on or after 1 January 2026, existing ships in scope complying not later than the first survey on or after 1 January 2028;
further amendments aimed at new energy vehicles were still in development, so the regulatory answer is partly delivered and continuing.

blocks.h: 6. b) Measures by stakeholder to address the safety challenges

ul: IMO - complete the new-energy-vehicle amendments, keep IMDG provisions current, maintain interim guidance meanwhile;
flag State and class - approve and survey the amended detection, suppression and boundary arrangements, and issue guidance ahead of the compliance dates;
shipper, manufacturer and packer - correct IMDG classification, packing and marking, state-of-charge control, testing and quality control, and no offering of damaged, defective or recalled batteries;
port and terminal - screen and refuse visibly damaged vehicles, check declared state of charge, separate electric vehicles in marshalling areas, inform the ship promptly;
ship operator - a written stowage and segregation policy, limits on charging on board, training in lithium fire behaviour, vehicle-deck drills, thermal imaging, and a plan that assumes re-ignition;

ship's staff - verify cargo against the declaration, maintain detection and drencher readiness, patrol during and after loading, and fight fire by early activation of fixed systems and boundary cooling rather than entering a loaded deck;
insurers and industry bodies - loss-prevention guidance, incident and near-miss data sharing, and premium signals rewarding compliant stowage - the same data that feeds the next FSA.

blocks.p: The 10-mark limb is a method question, and method questions are marked on whether the method is visible. Naming the five steps and then walking the cargo through them is what separates a top answer from a general essay about battery fires. Step 5 is where most candidates stop short: an FSA that produces no recommendation has not been applied, so ending with the actual resolutions is what closes the loop.

Before FSA, IMO regulation was largely reactive - a casualty happened, and a rule followed. FSA was introduced after the Herald of Free Enterprise and Piper Alpha era to allow the Organization to act proactively and proportionately, on evidence rather than on the emotional weight of the most recent disaster, and to be able to say publicly why a proposed rule was or was not worth its cost. That is why the Guidelines insist on auditability, traceability and the explicit reporting of uncertainty: an FSA is as much an accountability document as a technical one.

blocks.h: The lithium hazard in engineering terms

blocks.p: Thermal runaway begins when a cell's internal temperature passes the point at which exothermic decomposition of the electrolyte and cathode outpaces heat loss. The decomposition liberates oxygen from the cathode material, which is why the reaction sustains itself without air and why smothering agents - CO2, foam blanket, an inert atmosphere - do not stop it. Cooling is the only lever the ship holds, and it works by removing heat from cells that have not yet reached onset temperature, so its real objective is to stop propagation to neighbouring vehicles rather than to extinguish the cell already in runaway. That is also why re-ignition is normal rather than surprising: the cells that were merely heated may still cross the threshold hours later.

blocks.h: Vehicles, containers and packages are three different regulatory problems

ul: Cells and batteries as cargo - dangerous goods under the IMDG Code, class 9, with UN numbers such as 3480 and 3481 for lithium-ion and 3090 and 3091 for lithium-metal, subject to packing, marking, documentation and segregation.
Batteries in or with equipment - the same UN family but different provisions, and often carried under exceptions.

A battery electric vehicle - carried as a vehicle, not as a declared dangerous goods package. This is the regulatory gap: the ship may know exactly how many tonnes of declared lithium cells she has in containers, and not know how much energy is sitting on the vehicle deck.
Describing FSA as a shipboard risk assessment. Read the circular's title.
Listing the five steps and then never using them - a hazard essay wearing an FSA hat.
Saying water must never be used on a lithium fire. Cooling and boundary protection with copious water is the accepted tactic.
Saying the fire can be smothered with CO2. The reaction supplies its own oxidant.
Declaring the fire out when flames stop. Re-ignition must be assumed and monitored for.
Treating a battery electric vehicle as though it were declared dangerous goods, or vice versa.
'In vehicles and containers and in RORO ships' - three carriage modes are named deliberately, and an answer that only discusses containers has ignored a third of the question.
'Application of formal safety assessment' - the mark is in the application, not the definition.
Limb (b) says stakeholders, plural. An answer confined to what the ship's staff should do cannot score well; the chain begins at the cell manufacturer.
A car on your vehicle deck is smoking. What are your first four actions?
Why will CO2 not put out a lithium-ion fire?
How would you know a battery electric vehicle had been loaded?
What does 'individually identifiable' mean in a detection system, and why does it matter here?
When can you say this fire is out?

blocks.p: The method as a funnel: what could go wrong, how bad and how often, what could we do, is it worth it, what do we recommend. The hazard in four words that each defeat a normal tactic: self-oxidising, propagating, venting, re-igniting. The remedy chain for limb (b) runs down the supply chain: regulator, class, shipper, terminal, operator, ship.

The answer therefore explains how the FSA method applies to this cargo and identifies the FIRESAFE programme and the resulting amendments as the risk-based work that was actually done; it does not assert that a formal FSA submission on lithium batteries exists. blocks.p: Modern salvage law rests on the International Convention on Salvage, 1989, in force since 14 July 1996, which replaced a purely property-based regime with one that also rewards protection of the environment. Its principles are:

ul: Voluntary service - the salvor owes no pre-existing duty; a tug already under a towage contract is not salving.
Real danger to a vessel or other property in navigable waters.
"No cure, no pay" - by Article 12, only operations which have had a useful result give rise to payment.

A reward fixed to encourage salvage, on the ten criteria of Article 13(1) - salved value; skill and efforts in preventing environmental damage; measure of success; degree of danger; skill in salving vessel, property and life; time, expenses and losses; risk of liability; promptness; availability of salvage equipment; and its readiness, efficiency and value. The reward may not exceed the salved value.

Environmental protection in its own right - where the vessel or cargo threatened environmental damage, Article 14 gives the salvor special compensation (his expenses) even with no Article 13 reward, increasable by up to 30%, and by a tribunal to a maximum of 100% of expenses.

Duties both ways (Article 8) - the salvor to exercise due care, minimise environmental damage and accept other salvors when reasonably required; the owner and master to co-operate and accept redelivery when reasonably requested.

blocks.p: In practice salvage is contracted on Lloyd's Open Form; because Article 14 proved slow and contentious to assess, the industry added the SCOPIC clause in 2000 - an agreed tariff with a fixed uplift, which the salvor may invoke in place of Article 14.

General Average is the principle that where a sacrifice or extraordinary expenditure is made deliberately to save a common maritime adventure, the loss is shared by all the interests saved rather than left on the party that bore it. Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules: there is a general average act "when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure". In Indian law a general average loss is defined at section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. Every element must be present: a real common peril; an extraordinary act, not one the ship was already bound to do; intentional and voluntary; reasonable; for the common safety, not one interest alone; and property saved to contribute. The Rules are contractual, not statutory - they bind only because the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them, which is why those documents name the edition.

The party who made the sacrifice or incurred the expenditure is entitled to contribution from every interest saved - ship, cargo and freight at risk - rateably on their contributory values at the time and place the adventure ends. It requires the Rule A elements and a loss that is a direct consequence of the act. It is defeated by the actionable fault of the claiming party: a shipowner whose unseaworthiness caused the casualty recovers nothing, because the Rules preserve the other parties' defences. Since cargo is released before the adjustment is finished, the owner exercises a lien on cargo and takes security first - an average bond with a general average guarantee from cargo underwriters, or a cash deposit.

"Artificial" general average describes allowances which the numbered Rules permit although they do not satisfy the strict common-safety test in Rule A. The clearest examples are port of refuge expenses and the wages and maintenance of crew during the detention there: once the ship has reached a place of safety the common safety is already secured, so that further expenditure is incurred for the common benefit of completing the adventure rather than to escape peril. The Rules allow it as a practical commercial compromise. The term is practitioner usage, not a defined category of the Rules, and the examinable point is the distinction it marks - general average in principle rests on common safety, while in practice the Rules also extend it to common benefit.

Adjustment turns the casualty into a settled apportionment, carried out by an average adjuster - appointed and paid by the shipowner but required to act impartially between all interests. The adjuster neither declares general average nor determines liability. The work is to collect security before cargo is released; decide which sacrifices and expenditures are allowable under the applicable edition; ascertain contributory values at the termination of the adventure; apportion rateably; and issue the general average statement. Large casualties take years, which is why the security taken at the outset matters.

The adjustment is not binding. It is a skilled statement of account and strong evidence, but any interest - most often cargo underwriters - may contest it. The usual grounds are that there was no general average act at all; that the expenditure was not extraordinary or not reasonable; that an allowance is not permitted by the incorporated edition; that contributory values or allowances are wrongly assessed; that the wrong edition has been applied; or, most powerfully, that the casualty was caused by the actionable fault of the claiming party, so that no contribution is due at all. It is resolved by negotiation, arbitration, or the courts of the jurisdiction the contract of carriage provides for.

The marks are printed, which is a gift: 4 + 4 + 8. Give salvage a quarter of the answer and no more, define General Average tightly, and then spend half the answer on the four named sub-items. The commonest way to lose marks here is to write a long general essay on general average and then deal with entitlement, artificial, adjustment and contestation in a sentence each. Each of those four is worth about two marks - give each of them its own heading so the examiner can see all four have been answered.

blocks.h: The four sub-items are a lifecycle - use that

blocks.p: They are not four unrelated definitions. Read in order they describe what happens after a casualty: who may claim (entitlement), what may be claimed even though strict principle would exclude it (artificial), how the claim is worked out (adjustment), and how it is fought (contestation). Presenting them as a sequence turns a list into an argument, and it makes them far easier to recall.

This is the item most candidates cannot place, and precision matters. Artificial general average is not fraud and not a fictitious claim. It is the name practitioners give to allowances the numbered Rules permit even though the common safety has already been achieved - classically port of refuge expenses and crew wages and maintenance during the detention. The underlying distinction is common safety (the Rule A test) against common benefit (completing the adventure). Say that distinction explicitly and the mark is earned. Be careful to present the term as accepted usage rather than as a defined category of the Rules, because it is not defined in them.

blocks.h: Salvage and General Average are different things

blocks.p: They meet - a salvage award is commonly allowed in general average and apportioned across the interests - but they are not the same. Salvage is a reward to a stranger for a voluntary service to property in danger, governed by a convention. General Average is a sharing of loss between parties already joined in one adventure, governed by contract. A candidate who blurs them will struggle with 'artificial', because the reason salvage and port of refuge expenses need special treatment is precisely that they sit at the join.

ul: Treating the York-Antwerp Rules as law. They are contractual and apply only because a bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them; the edition named in the contract governs.
Saying the average adjuster declares general average or decides liability. The shipowner, normally through the master, declares it; the adjuster apportions it.
Forgetting security. Without an average bond and a GA guarantee, the shipowner has released the cargo and lost the lien that protects the claim.
Omitting the actionable fault defence, which is the single most important limit on entitlement and the strongest ground of contestation.
Writing that a salvor is always paid. Article 12 is "no cure, no pay" - and the Article 14 environmental exception exists precisely because that rule was leaving environmental salvage unrewarded.
Quoting an Article 13 reward that exceeds the salved value. It cannot.

blocks.p:
"The salvor saved the environment but not the ship - what does he get?" Not an Article 13 reward, because there was no useful result in property terms. He may claim Article 14 special compensation - his expenses, increasable by up to 30% and by a tribunal up to 100% - or, if invoked, SCOPIC remuneration under the contract.

"Is the adjuster's statement final?" No. It is evidence, not a judgment, and it can be contested on the grounds above.

"Which edition of the Rules applies?" Whichever the contract of carriage incorporates. YAR 2016 was adopted by the CMI in May 2016 and BIMCO forms refer to it, but older contracts still commonly incorporate YAR 1994.

ul: State Rule A. "There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure."
Where is general average defined in Indian law? Section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.
Give two examples of artificial general average. Port of refuge expenses, and crew wages and maintenance during the detention there.
What security does the shipowner take before releasing cargo? An average bond from cargo interests and a general average guarantee from their underwriters, or a cash deposit.
What is SCOPIC and why does it exist? A contractual tariff annexed to Lloyd's Open Form, introduced in 2000, because assessing Article 14 special compensation proved slow and contentious.
Can a shipowner claim contribution if his own unseaworthiness caused the casualty? No - actionable fault defeats the claim.

General Average: Rule A, then the four printed items as a lifecycle - who claims, what counts, who works it out, who fights it (steps 3 to 6).

blocks.p: Two points of honesty. First, "artificial general average" is practitioner terminology, not a defined term of the York-Antwerp Rules. It is used consistently in the adjusting profession to describe allowances made on a common-benefit basis where the strict Rule A common-safety test is not met, and this answer explains it in those terms; a candidate should present it as accepted usage and explain the underlying common safety versus common benefit distinction, which is what the mark is really for. Second, which edition of the Rules applies is a matter of the contract, not of law, so no answer can assert that YAR 2016 governs a given casualty. The Salvage Convention figures - the useful-result rule, the ten Article 13 criteria, the salved-value ceiling and the 30% and 100% uplifts in Article 14 - have been read in the Convention text and are stated exactly. questions.understand_first: Salvage and general average both answer the question "who pays when a ship gets into trouble", but they answer it about different people. Salvage is about paying an outsider who chose to come and help. General average is about splitting a deliberate loss between the people who were already in the adventure together. Once that split is clear, the four sub-items are simply the life of a general average claim: who may claim, what the Rules let them claim, how it is calculated, and how it is fought.

blocks.h: 1. What the owner is exposed to

blocks.p: Identify the exposures before naming any cover: loss of the ship; loss of the cargo; oil pollution from persistent cargo oil and bunkers; salvage, already under way; wreck location, marking and removal; crew death or injury; and claims by the coastal state and third parties. She sank in the territorial sea, where by UNCLOS Article 2 the coastal state has full sovereignty - so its law and its convention obligations govern what may be demanded of the owner.

ul: H&M insures the owner's own property interest in the ship, on standard terms such as the Institute Time Clauses (Hulls), the International Hull Clauses or the Nordic Plan. Explosion is ordinarily an insured peril.

Because the vessel sank, the claim will be an actual total loss where the ship is irretrievably lost, or a constructive total loss where recovery and repair would exceed the insured value - in which case the owner serves a notice of abandonment.
Sue and labour expenses reasonably incurred to avert or minimise the loss are recoverable, which is significant here because salvage was in progress.
General average contributions and salvage charges falling on the ship are recoverable under the policy.

blocks.p: P&I is the mutual cover for third-party liabilities that H&M does not touch, and in this casualty it does most of the work: oil pollution, wreck removal where required by law, cargo liability, crew death, injury and repatriation, damage to fixed and floating objects, and certain fines. Clubs in the International Group share risk through a pooling and reinsurance structure, which is what makes a casualty of this size insurable. The club also issues the "blue cards" on which the state issues the ship's compulsory insurance certificates.

ul: CLC 1992 governs pollution damage from persistent oil carried in bulk as cargo. Liability is strict and is channelled to the registered owner; the owner may limit by tonnage unless the damage resulted from his personal act or omission committed with intent, or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result. It requires compulsory insurance and a certificate, and gives claimants a direct right of action against the insurer. It applies to pollution damage in the territory, territorial sea and EEZ of a State Party.

Fund Convention 1992 provides a second tier where CLC compensation is unavailable or insufficient, and the Supplementary Fund Protocol 2003 a third tier for states that join it. Together these are the reason a tanker owner's exposure is finite while claimants remain compensated.

Bunkers Convention 2001 covers bunker pollution where CLC does not - principally non-tankers and tankers in ballast. It imposes strict liability on a broadly defined shipowner and requires compulsory insurance for ships over 1,000 GT. For a laden tanker such as this VLCC, CLC covers bunker-oil damage as well, so Bunkers is the fallback rather than the primary regime.

blocks.h: 5. Wreck removal, salvage and global limitation

ul: Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks, 2007 (in force 14 April 2015) makes the registered owner strictly liable for locating, marking and removing a hazardous wreck, with compulsory insurance and a certificate for ships of 300 GT and above and a direct action against the insurer. It applies by default in the exclusive economic zone; it reaches the territorial sea only where the state has opted to extend it - so whether it governs here depends on that coastal state.

Salvage. The salvors' claim continues under the Salvage Convention 1989 - an Article 13 reward if there was a useful result, otherwise Article 14 special compensation, or SCOPIC remuneration if invoked under Lloyd's Open Form. The sinking does not extinguish the claim.

Global limitation. The LLMC 1976, as amended by the 1996 Protocol, allows the owner to constitute a limitation fund by tonnage for most maritime claims. Some states exclude wreck removal claims from limitation by reservation, and limitation is lost on the same conduct test as under CLC.

blocks.p: None of this is unconditional. Cover can be prejudiced by unseaworthiness or want of due diligence, breach of a class or trading warranty, non-disclosure - the contract is one of utmost good faith, governed in Indian law by sections 19 and 20 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 - and wilful misconduct. A tank explosion at once raises questions about inert gas operation, tank atmosphere control and the safety management system, and those answers decide both whether the policy responds and whether the owner keeps his right to limit. The immediate duties are practical: notify H&M and the club, preserve evidence, appoint surveyors, co-operate with the coastal and flag state investigations, and concede nothing on liability.

The question prints its own two limbs, (a) insurance and (b) conventions, so give them roughly eight marks each and keep them visibly separate. The strongest opening is the one used here - a short paragraph identifying the exposures before naming any cover. It shows you understand that insurance and conventions are two different answers to the same question: what happens to the money.

blocks.h: The two-axis idea that organises everything

blocks.p: There are two independent axes and candidates constantly collapse them. Axis one: whose loss. H&M covers the owner's own property; P&I covers his liability to others. Axis two: liability versus compensation. The conventions decide whether the owner is liable and how much he can limit; insurance decides who pays. CLC does not insure anybody - it imposes strict liability and then requires the owner to carry insurance for it. Say that sentence and you have the examiner's attention.

blocks.h: Why CLC and not Bunkers leads here

blocks.p: This is a VLCC and the casualty involved a tank explosion, so it was carrying persistent oil in bulk as cargo. That puts the casualty squarely inside CLC 1992, which then also covers the ship's bunker oil. The Bunkers Convention 2001 exists for the cases CLC leaves out - non-tankers, and tankers in ballast. Leading with Bunkers on a laden VLCC signals that the candidate has learned a list rather than a regime.

blocks.h: The territorial sea detail is deliberate

blocks.p: The examiner put the sinking in the territorial sea of a coastal state, not on the high seas, and that is worth marks. By UNCLOS Article 2 the coastal state has sovereignty there, so its law applies directly. It also creates the one genuine trap in the question: the Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention applies automatically in the EEZ, and to the territorial sea only if the state has opted to extend it. Saying "Nairobi applies" flatly is an overstatement; saying it applies if that state has extended it is precise.

ul: Treating CLC as a form of insurance. It is a liability convention with a compulsory-insurance requirement attached.
Confusing the tiers. CLC is the owner, the 1992 Fund is the second tier, the Supplementary Fund is the third for states that join it.

Assuming the owner can always limit. Limitation is lost where the damage resulted from his personal act or omission with intent, or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result.
Forgetting that the salvors still have a claim after the ship sinks - a useful result may be absent, but Article 14 or SCOPIC may not be.
Writing as though cover is automatic. Unseaworthiness, breach of warranty and non-disclosure are exactly the issues a tank explosion raises.
Ignoring the cargo interests entirely. The cargo owner has lost a VLCC parcel of oil and will be claiming.

blocks.p:
"The ship sank - is it a total loss?" Distinguish. An actual total loss is where the ship is destroyed or irretrievably deprived; a constructive total loss is where recovery and repair would cost more than the insured value, and it requires a notice of abandonment. The bare fact of sinking does not decide which.

"Who pays for removing the wreck?" The registered owner, strictly, under the Nairobi Convention where it applies - and his P&I club in practice, subject to the certificate and direct action.

"Does the salvage claim die with the ship?" No. Article 13 needs a useful result, but Article 14 special compensation and SCOPIC exist precisely for the case where the property is lost but the environment was protected.

ul: Difference between H&M and P&I? H&M is your own hull; P&I is your liability to third parties, on a mutual basis.
On whom does CLC channel liability? The registered owner, strictly, with a right to limit by tonnage and compulsory insurance behind it.
When did the Nairobi Convention enter into force, and where does it apply? 14 April 2015; in the EEZ by default and in the territorial sea only where the state extends it.
What is a blue card? The club's confirmation of cover, on the strength of which a state issues the ship's compulsory insurance certificate under CLC or Bunkers.
What breaks the right to limit? The owner's personal act or omission committed with intent, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result.
What would you do in the first hour as Chief Engineer? Preserve records and data, secure the evidence, report through the master to owners, club and flag state, and give nothing away on liability.

blocks.p: OWN - OTHERS - OIL - WRECK - LIMIT. Own property is H&M and total loss (step 2). Others is P&I (step 3). Oil is CLC, Fund and Supplementary Fund, with Bunkers as the fallback (step 4). Wreck brings in Nairobi and the continuing salvage claim (step 5). Limit is LLMC, and the conduct that destroys it (steps 5 and 6).

questions.understand_first: Two different systems are at work and they answer different questions. The conventions decide whether the owner is liable at all, to whom, and how much of it he can cap. Insurance decides who actually finds the money once that is settled. CLC is often misread as a form of cover, but it is the opposite - it imposes strict liability on the owner and then obliges him to insure it. Keep those two apart and the whole answer falls into place.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish H&M from P&I in one sentence each.
retrieval_cards.answer: H&M insures the owner's own property interest in the ship. P&I is mutual cover for his liabilities to third parties - pollution, wreck removal, cargo, crew and certain fines.
retrieval_cards.why: Own loss versus liability to others is the first organising axis.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is CLC 1992 a form of insurance?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It is a liability convention: strict liability channelled to the registered owner, with a right to limit by tonnage, and a compulsory insurance requirement plus a direct right of action against the insurer attached to it.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most common conceptual error in this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does CLC rather than the Bunkers Convention lead on this casualty?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because a VLCC that suffered a tank explosion was laden with persistent oil in bulk as cargo. CLC then covers the bunker oil as well. The Bunkers Convention 2001 exists for non-tankers and tankers in ballast.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Actual or constructive total loss?
retrieval_cards.answer: Actual where the ship is destroyed or the owner is irretrievably deprived of her. Constructive where the cost of recovery and repair would exceed the insured value - which requires a notice of abandonment to the underwriters.
retrieval_cards.why: Sinking alone does not decide which applies.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does the Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention apply?
retrieval_cards.answer: In the exclusive economic zone by default, and in the territorial sea only where the State Party has opted to extend it. In force 14 April 2015; certificate and compulsory insurance for ships of 300 GT and above.
retrieval_cards.why: The territorial sea detail in the question is deliberate - do not say it applies flatly.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the three tiers of oil pollution compensation for a laden tanker?
retrieval_cards.answer: CLC 1992 - the owner and his insurer. The 1992 Fund - second tier. The Supplementary Fund Protocol 2003 - third tier, for states party to it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What conduct destroys the owner's right to limit liability?
retrieval_cards.answer: Damage resulting from his personal act or omission committed with intent to cause such damage, or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result.
retrieval_cards.why: The same test appears in CLC and in the LLMC - learn the wording.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the salvors' claim survive the ship sinking?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes. Article 13 needs a useful result, but Article 14 special compensation and, if invoked, SCOPIC remuneration exist precisely for the case where the property is lost but environmental damage was prevented or minimised.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What could stop the insurance responding at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: Unseaworthiness or want of due diligence, breach of a class or trading warranty, non-disclosure or misrepresentation, and wilful misconduct. A tank explosion immediately puts inert gas operation and the safety management system in issue.

sources: PRIMARY: IMO resolution MEPC.378(80), adopted 7 July 2023 at MEPC 80 - '2023 Guidelines for the control and management of ships' biofouling to minimize the transfer of invasive aquatic species'. Operative clause 1 ADOPTS the Guidelines; clause 2 REQUESTS Member States to take urgent action in applying them; clause 3 AGREES to keep them under review; clause 4 REVOKES resolution MEPC.207(62), the 2011 Guidelines. The instrument is RECOMMENDATORY - it requests, it does not require.

PRIMARY: MEPC.378(80) section 2 definitions - biofouling is the accumulation of aquatic organisms on surfaces and structures immersed in or exposed to the aquatic environment, and can include pathogens; microfouling is caused by bacteria, fungi, microalgae and protozoans and creates a biofilm, also called a slime layer; macrofouling is visible plants and animals such as barnacles, tubeworms, mussels, algal fronds, bryozoans and sea squirts; an anti-fouling system (AFS) is a coating, paint, surface treatment, surface or device used to control or prevent attachment of organisms; a marine growth prevention system (MGPS) is an AFS used to prevent accumulation in niche areas or other surfaces; invasive aquatic species are non-native species which may pose threats to human, animal and plant life, economic and cultural activities and the aquatic environment; fouling rating is a number allocated to a defined inspection area from a visual assessment; capture is the containment, collection and removal of biofouling material and waste substances detached during cleaning; biofouling pressure is the accumulation rate, which differs regionally and seasonally.

PRIMARY: MEPC.378(80) paragraph 10.1 - it is recommended that every ship have a ship-specific BFMP under the responsibility of shipowners, ship operators and shipmasters; 10.2 - an effective BFMP should contribute to maintaining a recommended fouling rating of 1 or less, as described in chapter 8.

PRIMARY: MEPC.378(80) paragraph 10.3, items .1 to .13 - the BFMP should include the officer or position responsible (the Guidelines give chief engineer as the example); details of the AFS installed and where; recommended operating conditions suited to the AFS including temperature, salinity and speed; expected AFC efficacy through its lifetime; description of monitoring of biofouling risk parameters; the cleaning regime if any; details of hull and niche areas where biofouling may accumulate; the schedule for fixed inspections; procedures for reactive cleaning triggered by inspection results; a contingency action plan based on specific triggers; the regime for repair, maintenance and renewal of the AFS per the manufacturer's instructions; the process for monitoring and maintaining the MGPS; and details of the documentation and reports required. Paragraph 10.7 requires the BFMP to be reviewed after inspections and cleaning and updated if the management actions are ineffective or deficient. Paragraph 10.8 - a form of BFMP is set out in appendix 3.

PRIMARY: MEPC.378(80) paragraph 11.1 to 11.5 - record-keeping in a BFRB is the responsibility of shipowners, ship operators and/or shipmasters; it is recommended that the BFRB be retained on board for the LIFE OF THE SHIP; it may be maintained physically or electronically and may be stand-alone or integrated into existing manuals or planned maintenance systems; and paragraph 11.4 lists the eight categories of entry, reproduced in the answer. A form of BFRB is set out in appendix 4.

PRIMARY: MEPC.378(80) paragraph 1.8 - the related frameworks are the BWM Convention 2004 and the AFS Convention 2001; paragraph 1.9 - biofouling management supports hydrodynamic performance and energy efficiency, linked to the SEEMP guidelines (MEPC.346(78)) and the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy (MEPC.377(80)); paragraph 1.10 - the GEF-UNDP-IMO GloFouling Partnerships Project.

blocks.h: 1. What biofouling is, and the two problems it creates

blocks.p: The 2023 Guidelines define biofouling as the accumulation of aquatic organisms on surfaces immersed in or exposed to the aquatic environment, and note that it can include pathogens. Microfouling is the biofilm or slime layer; macrofouling is the visible growth that follows - barnacles, tubeworms, mussels, algal fronds, bryozoans and sea squirts. It settles on the hull and, critically, in niche areas: sea chests and gratings, thruster tunnels, propeller and shaft, rudder stock and hinge, dry-dock support strips, anodes and transducers. It creates two separate problems - ship performance for the owner, and invasive aquatic species for the receiving ecosystem - and limb (a) asks about both.

ul: Added frictional resistance - hull roughness rises, so more delivered power is needed for the same speed. This begins at the slime stage; macrofouling is not needed for a measurable penalty.
Higher fuel consumption or lost speed - the ship either burns more to hold the schedule or slows at constant power.

Degraded carbon standing - more fuel per tonne-mile worsens the operational carbon indicator and works against the SEEMP. The Guidelines expressly link biofouling management to energy efficiency and the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy.
Machinery consequences - fouled sea chests, gratings and coolers reduce seawater flow, raise pump load and lift cooler outlet temperatures. This is an engine-room problem, not only a hull one.
Manoeuvring and appendage effects from growth on propeller, rudder and thruster tunnels.
Cost - more frequent cleaning and docking, shorter AFS life, and exposure under charter-party speed and consumption warranties.

Transfer of invasive aquatic species. This is the reason the Guidelines exist. Biofouling is a major vector: non-native organisms carried on the hull and in niche areas may establish in a new ecosystem and threaten human, animal and plant life, economic and cultural activities and the aquatic environment. Niche areas are the highest risk because they are sheltered and often missed.
Increased air emissions. The extra fuel burned to overcome added resistance is additional CO2, NOx and SOx.

Impacts of the countermeasure itself. Anti-fouling systems release biocides, which is why the AFS Convention 2001 controls them; and in-water cleaning can discharge viable organisms and biocide-laden paint particles, which is why the Guidelines require captured waste to be disposed of safely and in an environmentally sound manner.
Regulatory and commercial exposure. Some States apply their own biofouling requirements on arrival, and a fouled hull can mean cleaning at anchor, delay or refused entry.

A risk-based, ship-specific approach - the central change in the 2023 Guidelines. The ship monitors biofouling risk parameters (operating profile, idle time, trading area, temperature, salinity, biofouling pressure) and lets the resulting risk set inspection and cleaning intervals, instead of a fixed regime.
Proactive cleaning, or grooming, rather than reactive - frequent gentle removal of biofilm before macrofouling establishes, which protects the coating and avoids releasing established organisms.

Better anti-fouling systems - foul-release, low-surface-energy silicone and hydrogel coatings that resist adhesion rather than relying on biocide, with the AFS chosen to match ship type, operating profile and conditions.
Hull and propeller performance monitoring - measuring the power-speed relationship so cleaning is triggered by evidence rather than by the calendar.
Robotic in-water inspection and cleaning with capture, filtering and retaining removed material, and approval regimes for cleaning systems.
Design measures - minimising and giving access to niche areas at newbuilding stage, and fitting MGPS to sea chests and internal seawater systems.
Contingency action plans on defined triggers, such as an extended idle period in an area of high biofouling pressure.

blocks.h: 5. (c) How a ship-specific Biofouling Management Plan minimises biofouling

blocks.p: The Guidelines recommend that every ship have a ship-specific BFMP, under the responsibility of the shipowner, operator and master, and give it a measurable objective: it should contribute to maintaining a fouling rating of 1 or less. It minimises biofouling not by being a document but by converting management into named duties, thresholds and triggers:

ul: It fixes accountability. It identifies the officer or position responsible - the Guidelines give chief engineer as the example - so the plan is implemented rather than filed.

It records what is fitted and how it must be operated. Details of the AFS and where it is installed, the operating conditions suited to it including temperature, salinity and speed, and its expected efficacy over its life - so the ship does not unknowingly operate outside the coating's design envelope.
It maps where fouling will occur. The hull and niche areas where biofouling may accumulate, so inspection looks in the right places.

It turns monitoring into action. A description of the biofouling risk parameters monitored, a schedule of fixed inspections, a cleaning regime, and procedures for reactive cleaning triggered by inspection results.
It plans for the abnormal. A contingency action plan based on specific triggers from the monitored parameters.
It maintains the defences. A regime for repair, maintenance and renewal of the AFS to the manufacturer's instructions, and a process for monitoring and maintaining the MGPS.
It closes the loop. It specifies the documentation required, and the plan itself must be reviewed after inspections and cleaning and updated if the measures prove ineffective or deficient.

blocks.h: 6. (d) Entries in the Biofouling Record Book

blocks.p: Record-keeping is the responsibility of the shipowner, operator and/or master. It is recommended that the BFRB be retained on board for the life of the ship; it may be kept physically or electronically, and may be stand-alone or integrated into existing manuals or the planned maintenance system. All biofouling management activities should be recorded, including:

ol: Details of repair and maintenance to the AFS - date, location, areas of the ship affected, and the percentage of the ship recoated - in addition to entries in the International Anti-fouling System Certificate.
Details of repair and maintenance to the MGPS - date, location and areas affected.
In-water inspections - initial date, final date, duration in hours or days and location, including the inspection report.
Cleaning, in water or in dry dock - initial date, final date, duration and location, including a cleaning report.
Details of when the ship has been operating outside its normal operating profile, including any lay-up or extended inactive periods.
Details of the performance monitoring parameters used to determine inspection intervals.
A copy of the cleaning report, if applicable.
A description of contingency actions taken, including date, time and location.

blocks.p: One qualification belongs in the answer and carries marks. The Biofouling Guidelines, the BFMP and the BFRB are recommendatory: MEPC.378(80) adopts the Guidelines and requests Member States to apply them. Unlike the Oil Record Book under MARPOL Annex I, the BFRB is not a statutory record book under a convention - although individual flag States, port States and charterers increasingly require it, which is what gives it practical force.

Four printed limbs at four marks each, so the answer must be four visibly separate and roughly equal blocks. The commonest way to lose marks here is to spend half the answer on limb (a) - biofouling consequences are easy to write about at length - and then compress (c) and (d), which are the two limbs where the marks are most reliably earned because they have definite content in the Guidelines. Limb (a) is worth splitting explicitly into performance and environment, because the question names both and an answer that blurs them looks like it only knows one.

blocks.h: The one qualification that separates a good answer

blocks.p: The 2023 Biofouling Guidelines are recommendatory, not mandatory. Resolution MEPC.378(80) adopts them and requests Member States to take urgent action in applying them; it revoked the 2011 Guidelines in MEPC.207(62). There is no MARPOL annex on biofouling. A candidate who writes that the Biofouling Record Book is required under MARPOL, or treats it as the equivalent of the Oil Record Book, has made a legal error in a question that is otherwise mostly descriptive - and it is exactly the kind of error an examiner uses to separate candidates. The honest position, which also shows commercial awareness, is that the instrument is voluntary at IMO level but is increasingly made binding in practice by flag State and port State requirements, by charterers and by regional arrival standards.

This reads like an environmental question, but half of it is engine-room work. The resistance penalty starts at the slime layer, before anything is visible, which is why performance monitoring rather than visual inspection is what detects it. The seawater side is the part candidates forget: fouling in sea chests, on gratings, in coolers and in the internal seawater system reduces flow, raises pump power and lifts cooler outlet temperatures, and the MGPS exists precisely to manage that. Naming the chief engineer's role is not flattery either - paragraph 10.3.1 of the Guidelines gives chief engineer as its own example of the responsible position, so saying so is citing the instrument, not guessing.

ul: Treating the Guidelines, the BFMP or the BFRB as mandatory. They are recommendatory under MEPC.378(80).

Confusing the AFS Convention 2001 (controls the harmful anti-fouling systems themselves) with the Biofouling Guidelines (manage the fouling). They are different instruments with opposite subjects, and only the first is a convention.
Confusing biofouling with ballast water. Both transfer invasive aquatic species, but the BWM Convention is a separate mandatory regime for a different vector.
Answering limb (a) on fuel consumption alone and never mentioning invasive aquatic species - which is the entire purpose of the Guidelines.
Quoting a specific fuel-penalty percentage. The figures published vary widely and the Guidelines set none; state the mechanism instead.
Ignoring niche areas. They are the highest-risk locations for species transfer and are named throughout the Guidelines.
For limb (d), listing plausible-sounding entries instead of the eight categories in paragraph 11.4. The limb says state the entries, so the marks are in the list.

blocks.p:
'Is the Biofouling Record Book like the Oil Record Book?' No, and this is the trap. The Oil Record Book is required by MARPOL Annex I and false entries are an offence. The BFRB is recommended by a voluntary IMO resolution. Say so, then add that flag States, port States and charterers increasingly require it.

'Your ship has been at anchor for six weeks off a tropical port. What does your plan say?' This is the contingency action plan in 10.3.10 - extended idle time in an area of high biofouling pressure is exactly the trigger it exists for, and the event is recordable in the BFRB as operating outside the normal operating profile.

'Can you just clean the hull in water?' Not without regard to where you are. In-water cleaning can release viable organisms and biocide-laden paint particles, the Guidelines require capture and environmentally sound disposal of the waste, and many States regulate or prohibit it in their waters.

'Which fouling rating should the plan achieve?' An effective BFMP should contribute to maintaining a fouling rating of 1 or less.

ul: Which resolution contains the current Biofouling Guidelines, and what did it replace? MEPC.378(80), adopted 7 July 2023, revoking MEPC.207(62).
Are they mandatory? No - the resolution requests Member States to apply them.

Difference between microfouling and macrofouling? Microfouling is the biofilm or slime layer from bacteria, fungi, microalgae and protozoans; macrofouling is the visible growth - barnacles, tubeworms, mussels, algae, bryozoans, sea squirts.
What is an MGPS and where is it fitted? A marine growth prevention system, an AFS used to prevent accumulation in niche areas and internal seawater systems such as sea chests.
Name five niche areas. Sea chests and gratings, bow thruster tunnels, propeller and shaft, rudder stock and hinge, dry-dock support strips, anodes, transducers, rope guards.
Who is responsible for the BFMP on board? The Guidelines identify the officer or position - chief engineer is their own example - with overall responsibility on the owner, operator and master.
How long is the BFRB kept? It is recommended that it be retained on board for the life of the ship.
Which two conventions sit alongside the Guidelines? The BWM Convention 2004 and the AFS Convention 2001.

blocks.p: Take the limbs as WHY - HOW - PLAN - PROVE. Why it matters: fuel and species. How it is being tackled now: risk-based, proactive, better coatings, monitoring, robots with capture, design. Plan: the BFMP names who, what is fitted, where it fouls, when to inspect, what triggers cleaning, and how it is reviewed. Prove: the BFRB records AFS work, MGPS work, inspections, cleaning, off-profile operation, monitoring parameters, cleaning reports and contingency actions. For limb (a) specifically: SHIP and SEA - the ship pays in fuel, the sea pays in species.

blocks.p: The status statement in this answer is taken from the operative clauses of MEPC.378(80) itself: it adopts the Guidelines, requests Member States to apply them, agrees to keep them under review and revokes MEPC.207(62). That is a recommendation, and the answer says so rather than allowing the detail of the BFMP and BFRB to imply a mandatory regime. Two things are deliberately not quantified. No fuel or resistance penalty percentage is given: published figures differ by an order of magnitude depending on fouling rating, hull form, speed and measurement method, and the Guidelines set none, so a number here would be false precision. No national arrival standard is quoted: several States operate their own biofouling requirements, these are live regulatory instruments revised independently of IMO, and reproducing a current threshold would be wrong within months - the same live-external-reference problem already recorded for war-risk listed areas and approved recycling facilities. The technology description in limb (b) rests partly on classification-society and industry guidance rather than on the resolution, and is recorded as authoritative secondary.

questions.understand_first: It helps to see that biofouling is two unrelated problems that happen to have the same cause. For the owner it is a fuel bill: a rough hull needs more power for the same speed, and that starts with the invisible slime layer, not with barnacles. For the receiving port it is an ecological problem: the organisms sitting in the sea chest are alive, and they get discharged into a new ecosystem. Almost every measure in the Guidelines serves both at once, which is why a voluntary environmental instrument gets adopted by owners anyway - keeping the hull clean pays for itself.
