blocks.p: Ship health and vector control are governed by the International Health Regulations (2005), a binding instrument of the World Health Organization, as amended in 2014, 2022 and 2024. The 2024 amendments entered into force on 19 September 2025. The IHR work through designated points of entry, competent authorities at those points, and a small set of ship documents.

ul: It makes the rules. WHO adopts the IHR and prescribes the model certificates in Annex 3 and the Ship Declaration of Health in Annex 8, so the documents are the same worldwide.

It identifies where vector control is needed. Under Annex 5, WHO publishes on a regular basis a list of areas where disinsection or other vector control measures are recommended for conveyances arriving from them, through temporary or standing recommendations.

It advises methods and materials. Where WHO has advised methods for disinsection, deratting, disinfection or decontamination, those should be used unless the competent authority is satisfied that others are as safe and reliable (Article 27), and States should accept measures applied elsewhere by WHO-advised methods.

It certifies and publishes. On a State Party's request WHO may, after appropriate investigation, certify that a port meets the IHR requirements (Article 20(4)), publishes certification guidelines and the list of certified ports (20(5)), and publishes the lists of authorized ports notified by States Parties (20(3)).

It provides technical guidance - notably the WHO Handbook for inspection of ships and issuance of ship sanitation certificates - and declares Public Health Emergencies of International Concern with temporary recommendations.
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare - the health authority for IHR purposes, under which the National IHR Focal Point sits.

Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), and under it the Port Health Organisation, headed by the Port Health Officer - the competent authority at the point of entry. It inspects ships, baggage, cargo and containers, supervises control measures and issues the ship sanitation certificates, working under the Indian Port Health Rules, 1955 with the IHR 2005.
Directorate General of Shipping, through its Maritime Health Branch, on the seafarer side - approving medical examiners and governing seafarers' medical fitness examination and certification.
Port authorities and the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways support these functions at the ports themselves.

Ship Sanitation Control Exemption Certificate (SSCEC) - issued where the competent authority is satisfied that the ship is free of infection and contamination, including vectors and reservoirs, so that no control measures are required (Article 39(6)).

Ship Sanitation Control Certificate (SSCC) - issued where control measures were required and have been satisfactorily completed, and it records the evidence found and the measures taken (Article 39(5)). Under Annex 5 the presence of vectors on board and the measures used to eradicate them are recorded on this certificate. If a satisfactory result could not be obtained, the authority notes that on the certificate (Article 39(7)).

blocks.p: Both follow the model in Annex 3, and they replaced the former Deratting and Deratting Exemption Certificates. Alongside them the master submits a Ship Declaration of Health under Article 37, to the model in Annex 8 - a declaration, not a certificate. Separately, and concerning the crew rather than the ship, seafarers hold medical fitness certificates under MLC 2006 and STCW.

blocks.h: 5. Issue in India, validity and extension

ul: In India they are issued by the Port Health Officer at a port authorized for the purpose and notified to WHO. Under Article 20(3) a State Party notifies which ports may issue the SSCC, which may issue the SSCEC only, and which may grant the one-month extension.
Validity: a maximum of six months, for both the SSCEC and the SSCC (Article 39(1)).
Extension: by one month, where the inspection or the required control measures cannot be accomplished at that port - the extension carries the ship to a port where the certificate can be obtained.

Where no valid certificate is produced, or evidence of a public health risk is found on board, the State Party may proceed under Article 27(1) - treating the ship as affected and requiring disinfection, decontamination, disinsection or deratting.
Control measures are to be carried out whenever possible when the ship and holds are empty, and for a ship in ballast before loading (Article 39(4)).

For Indian coastal trade calling where no Port Health Officer is available, DG Shipping has provided for a Statement of Compliance issued by an authorized medical examiner, to be endorsed at the earliest available opportunity.

blocks.p: Four separate questions are asked and each must be visibly answered - WHO's role, the national agencies, the certificates, and issue/validity/extension in India. Take them in the printed order and head each one. The final limb contains the two numbers the examiner is certainly looking for, six months and one month, so never let it be squeezed by a long essay on WHO.

blocks.h: The currency point that will separate answers

blocks.p: The IHR were amended in 2024 and those amendments entered into force on 19 September 2025 - before this paper was sat, and before the January and March 2026 settings of the same question. One visible consequence: Article 37 is now the "Ship Declaration of Health". In the original 2005 text it was the "Maritime Declaration of Health", and that older name is what almost every textbook, coaching note and older syllabus still uses. Both texts were compared directly for this answer: the original uses "Maritime Declaration of Health" throughout and never the new name; the consolidated amended text uses "Ship Declaration of Health" throughout and never the old one. Using the current name, and being able to say why it changed, is a cheap and genuine mark.

blocks.h: Ship health and crew health are two different systems

blocks.p: The question asks about "the ship and the crew", and the two run on separate tracks with separate authorities. Ship health is WHO and the IHR, administered in India by the Port Health Organisation under DGHS and the Ministry of Health, and evidenced by the SSCC or SSCEC. Crew health is MLC 2006 and STCW, administered in India by DG Shipping through approved medical examiners, and evidenced by seafarers' medical fitness certificates. Candidates routinely put DG Shipping in charge of ship sanitation certificates. It is not - the Port Health Officer issues those.

ul: Calling the SSCC/SSCEC a Deratting Certificate. Those were the predecessors under the earlier Regulations and were replaced under the IHR 2005 - the scope widened from rodents to all infection and contamination including vectors and reservoirs.
Saying the certificates are valid for six months extendable by six months. The extension is one month, and only where the inspection or control measures cannot be accomplished at that port.
Confusing the SSCC with the SSCEC. Exemption means no measures were needed; Control means measures were required and were completed.
Treating the Ship Declaration of Health as a certificate. It is a declaration by the master, to the Annex 8 model, and a State may dispense with it entirely under Article 37(4).
Naming WHO as an enforcement body. WHO recommends, certifies ports on request and publishes; the competent authority at the point of entry enforces.

blocks.p:
"Your certificate expired yesterday and the port cannot inspect - what happens?" The one-month extension in Article 39(1) exists precisely for this, and under Article 20(3)(c) States notify which of their ports may grant it, so that the ship can reach a port where the certificate is obtainable.

"When should the inspection be done?" Whenever possible with the ship and holds empty, and for a ship in ballast before loading - Article 39(4). Answering "any time" misses a printed requirement.

"What does WHO actually do about mosquitoes?" It publishes the list of areas where vector control is recommended for conveyances arriving from them, and advises the methods. States Parties then run vector control programmes at points of entry - to a minimum distance of 400 metres from the operational areas under Annex 5.

ul: Who issues the SSCC in India? The Port Health Officer, at a port authorized for the purpose and notified by India to WHO.
Under which ministry does the Port Health Organisation sit? The Directorate General of Health Services, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Validity and extension? Maximum six months; extendable by one month where the inspection or control measures cannot be accomplished at the port.
What is recorded on an SSCC? The evidence found and the control measures taken - including, under Annex 5, the presence of vectors on board and the measures used to eradicate them.
What happens if you cannot produce a valid certificate? The State Party may treat the ship as affected under Article 27(1) and require disinfection, decontamination, disinsection or deratting.
Which convention covers the crew's medical fitness rather than the ship's sanitation? MLC 2006, with STCW for certification - administered in India by DG Shipping.

blocks.p: RULE - AGENCY - PAPER - CLOCK. Rule: IHR 2005 as amended, WHO's role (steps 1 to 2). Agency: MoHFW, DGHS, Port Health Organisation and the Port Health Officer, with DG Shipping on the crew side (step 3). Paper: SSCEC, SSCC, and the Ship Declaration of Health (step 4). Clock: six months, plus one (step 5). Two numbers, two certificates, one declaration.

questions.understand_first: There are two health systems on a ship and the question runs across both. One protects the world from the ship - vectors, infection and contamination crossing borders in a hull - and that is WHO's International Health Regulations, enforced by a port health authority and evidenced by a ship sanitation certificate. The other protects the crew, and that is labour and training law administered by the shipping administration. Keeping those two apart is what makes the India limb straightforward: the Port Health Officer certifies the ship, DG Shipping certifies the seafarer.

blocks.p: The flag State's obligations sit in Part VII of UNCLOS, and the scheme is a bargain: a ship must have a nationality, that nationality gives one State exclusive jurisdiction over her on the high seas, and in exchange that State must actually govern her. Article 92 provides that a ship shall sail under the flag of one State only and is subject to its exclusive jurisdiction on the high seas; a ship sailing under two or more flags according to convenience may claim none of those nationalities and may be assimilated to a ship without nationality.

ul: Every State fixes the conditions for the grant of its nationality, for registration, and for the right to fly its flag - its own decision, not an international prescription.
Ships have the nationality of the State whose flag they are entitled to fly.
There must exist a genuine link between the State and the ship. UNCLOS does not define the term and no settled test has emerged, which is the origin of the open-registry debate.
The State shall issue to ships to which it has granted the right to fly its flag documents to that effect - in practice the certificate of registry.

Article 94(2)(a) makes the register itself an obligation: the flag State shall maintain a register of ships with the names and particulars of ships flying its flag, other than those excluded on account of small size.

blocks.h: 3. (b) Control of safety, pollution and social aspects

blocks.p: Article 94(1) is the governing sentence: every State shall effectively exercise its jurisdiction and control in administrative, technical and social matters over ships flying its flag. That is then made specific:

ul: Article 94(2)(b) - assume jurisdiction under internal law over each ship, and over its master, officers and crew, in respect of administrative, technical and social matters.

Article 94(3) - take the measures necessary to ensure safety at sea as regards (a) construction, equipment and seaworthiness; (b) manning, labour conditions and training of crews, taking into account applicable international instruments - this is the social limb; and (c) use of signals, maintenance of communications and prevention of collisions.

Article 94(4) - those measures must include survey by a qualified surveyor before registration and thereafter at appropriate intervals; a master and officers appropriately qualified, in particular in seamanship, navigation, communications and marine engineering; and that master, officers and crew are fully conversant with and required to observe the applicable international regulations on safety of life at sea, collision prevention, marine pollution and radio communications.

Article 94(5) - in taking these measures each State is required to conform to generally accepted international regulations, procedures and practices. This is the hinge that pulls SOLAS, MARPOL, Load Lines, STCW, COLREG and MLC into UNCLOS.

Article 94(6) - a State with clear grounds to believe proper control is not exercised may report to the flag State, which shall investigate and take remedial action; 94(7) requires an inquiry into every marine casualty on the high seas involving loss of life, serious injury to another State's nationals, or serious damage to ships, installations or the environment.

On pollution, Article 217 requires flag States to ensure compliance, adopt laws, prohibit their ships from sailing until they can comply, ensure certificates are carried, inspect periodically, institute proceedings irrespective of where the violation occurred, and provide penalties adequate in severity to discourage violations.

blocks.h: 4. (c) India's constitutional and legislative mechanism since ratification

blocks.p: India signed UNCLOS on 10 December 1982 and ratified it on 29 June 1995, the Convention itself having entered into force on 16 November 1994. Ratification binds India as a State, but it does not by itself create rights and duties inside India: India is a dualist jurisdiction, so a treaty obligation takes domestic effect only through legislation. Limb (c) is therefore properly answered in two layers - the constitutional power to legislate, and the statutes actually enacted under it.

ul: The constitutional layer. Article 253 empowers Parliament to make any law for the whole or any part of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with another country - and it does so notwithstanding the ordinary distribution of legislative powers, so implementing UNCLOS is not obstructed by the federal division. The subject matter is in any event Union business: Seventh Schedule, Union List entry 14 (entering into and implementing treaties), entry 21 (piracy and crimes on the high seas), entry 25 (maritime shipping and navigation) and entry 57 (fishing beyond territorial waters). Article 297 vests in the Union the resources of the territorial waters, continental shelf and exclusive economic zone and provides for their limits to be specified by law. Article 51(c), a Directive Principle, directs the State to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations.

The maritime zones statute. The Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and other Maritime Zones Act, 1976 declares India's zones and the rights exercised in them. Note that it was enacted in 1976 - before ratification in 1995 and before the Convention was concluded in 1982 - in anticipation of the Third UN Conference. India legislated first and ratified afterwards, which is worth saying on a question asking about the position 'since its ratification'.

The flag State statute, and the currency point. The registration, safety, pollution and social obligations in Articles 91 and 94 are carried into Indian law by the merchant shipping legislation. At the date of this paper the operative statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (Act No. 24 of 2025), which received assent on 18 August 2025 and was brought into force in its entirety on 15 March 2026 by S.O. 1244(E), repealing the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 by section 324(1). Registration and nationality are administered by the Registrars of Indian Ships at the ports of registry, who issue the certificate of registry; section 15 governs who may own an Indian vessel and section 16 bareboat charter-cum-demise registration.

The administration. The Directorate General of Shipping, under the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, working through the Mercantile Marine Departments, discharges survey, certification, manning, training and casualty functions and issues merchant shipping notices as the subordinate instrument layer.

Delegation and verification. Statutory survey and certification are largely delegated to recognized organizations under the RO Code with the Administration retaining oversight, which is how Article 94(4)'s survey duty is met in practice. India also exercises port State control under the Indian Ocean MOU, and is audited against the III Code under the IMO Member State Audit Scheme. Casualty investigations and formal inquiries give effect to Article 94(7).

blocks.h: 5. How flag State performance is itself checked

blocks.p: UNCLOS creates the duty but provides no audit. That gap is filled by the III Code and the IMO Member State Audit Scheme, mandatory since 1 January 2016, under which every Member State is periodically audited on how it discharges its flag, coastal and port State obligations. With port State control, that is what turns Article 94 into something measurable.

Three printed limbs, so three visible blocks, and the marks divide roughly evenly. Limbs (a) and (b) are pure UNCLOS recall and reward article numbers - 91, 92, 94 and 217. Limb (c) is where a candidate can distinguish themselves, because it asks how an abstract treaty duty is actually discharged by a named administration. The closing section on audit is optional but cheap, and it answers the obvious follow-up: who checks the flag State?

blocks.h: The currency point - and it is the opposite way round from January

blocks.p:
This paper was sat in April 2026, and that date decides limb (c). The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 received assent on 18 August 2025 and was brought into force in full on 15 March 2026 by S.O. 1244(E) of 10 March 2026, repealing the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 by section 324(1). April therefore falls after commencement, so the correct answer to limb (c) at the date of this paper is the 2025 Act.

This is worth dwelling on, because the identical question was set in January 2026 and the correct answer there was the 1958 Act - January fell two months before commencement. Same question, same verified facts, opposite answer, purely because of the sitting date. A candidate revising both papers should be able to say which Act applied at which sitting and why, and a candidate answering today should give the 2025 Act and add one sentence acknowledging that the 1958 Act governed until 15 March 2026. That single sentence is what shows command of the transition rather than of a memorised name.

blocks.h: The idea that makes limbs (a) and (b) easy

blocks.p: UNCLOS strikes a bargain. Article 92 gives the flag State something valuable - exclusive jurisdiction over its ships on the high seas, so no other State may interfere. Article 94 is the price: the flag State must effectively exercise that jurisdiction. Every specific duty is an instalment of that price. And Article 94(5) is the clever part - by requiring conformity with "generally accepted international regulations", it imports SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, COLREG and Load Lines into UNCLOS without listing one of them. If you can state the bargain and the hinge, you can reconstruct the rest.

ul: Answering limb (c) with the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 on a January 2026 paper. It had not commenced.
Claiming UNCLOS defines the genuine link. It requires one and does not define it - that indeterminacy is the point, and the origin of the open-registry argument.

Saying UNCLOS requires ships to comply with SOLAS and MARPOL by name. It does not name them; Article 94(5) requires conformity with generally accepted international regulations, which is how they come in.
Forgetting the social limb, which the question names explicitly. It is Article 94(3)(b) - manning, labour conditions and training - and it is where MLC 2006 and STCW attach.
Suggesting that authorising a recognized organization transfers responsibility. It transfers the work; the Article 94 duty stays with the Administration, which must monitor the RO.
Omitting Article 217 and answering pollution purely from Article 94. Article 217 is the pollution enforcement article and carries the sailing prohibition and the adequate-penalty requirement.

blocks.p:
"A ship flies two flags - what is her nationality?" Under Article 92(2), a ship sailing under two or more flags according to convenience may claim none of those nationalities and may be assimilated to a ship without nationality.

"Who checks that the flag State does its job?" Other States may report under Article 94(6); port State control catches the ship; and the IMO Member State Audit Scheme, mandatory since 1 January 2016 against the III Code, audits the State itself.

"Does UNCLOS require surveys?" Yes, and this surprises candidates - Article 94(4)(a) expressly requires survey by a qualified surveyor before registration and thereafter at appropriate intervals.

ul: Which article gives exclusive flag State jurisdiction on the high seas? Article 92.
Which article sets the duties of the flag State? Article 94 - effective jurisdiction and control in administrative, technical and social matters.
Where is the genuine link requirement? Article 91(1), undefined by the Convention.
Which article deals with flag State enforcement on pollution? Article 217 - including prohibiting sailing until the ship can comply, and penalties adequate to discourage violations.
Who registers Indian ships and issues the certificate of registry? The Registrar of Indian Ships at the port of registry, under the Merchant Shipping Act.

Which Act applies at this sitting, and which applied at the January 2026 sitting of the same question? The Merchant Shipping Act 2025 now, in force since 15 March 2026; the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 then, repealed by section 324(1) of the 2025 Act.

blocks.p: 91 - 92 - 94 - 217, and remember what each is for: 91 nationality and the genuine link; 92 one flag, exclusive jurisdiction; 94 the duties, in three families - build (construction, equipment, seaworthiness), crew (manning, labour, training) and run (signals, communications, collision avoidance); 217 pollution enforcement. Then for India: statute, administration, registrar, surveyor, RO, audit.

blocks.p: The Indian material in limb (c) rests on two separately verified foundations. The constitutional propositions - Article 253, the Union List entries, Article 297 and Article 51(c) - are provisions of the Constitution of India and are stated at the level of what each provision does, without quoting text. The commencement facts for the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 were read in the Gazette during the QP2607 work: assent 18 August 2025, whole Act in force 15 March 2026 by S.O. 1244(E), the 1958 Act repealed by section 324(1). It is precisely those verified dates that establish that the 2025 Act is the answer at this sitting and that the 1958 Act was the answer in January. India's signature and ratification dates were taken from the United Nations treaty status record. Two things are deliberately not asserted. The subordinate rules made under the 2025 Act were still being brought forward when this answer was written, so the answer names the statute, the administration and the mechanism rather than enumerating current rules. And the answer does not claim that every provision of the 1958 Act's subordinate instrument layer has been remade - repeal of a parent Act does not automatically invalidate every rule made under it, savings provisions commonly preserve them, and that position was not independently established here.

questions.understand_first: UNCLOS makes a trade. It gives the flag State something no one else can have - exclusive jurisdiction over its ships on the high seas - and then spends Article 94 setting out what the State must do to deserve it. That is why the duties read like a list of everything a maritime administration does: register, survey, certify, man, investigate. And rather than listing the technical conventions, Article 94(5) simply requires conformity with generally accepted international regulations, which is how SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW and the rest are pulled in without being named.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does Article 217 add on pollution?

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does authorising a recognized organization discharge the flag State's duty?
retrieval_cards.answer: It delegates the work, not the responsibility. The Administration authorises ROs under the RO Code to survey and certify on its behalf, but retains the Article 94 duty and must monitor and audit them.

blocks.h: 1. (a) The mandatory basis in SOLAS and MARPOL

ul: SOLAS regulation XI-1/6 is the operative provision. Adopted by resolution MSC.257(84), it makes Parts I and II of the Casualty Investigation Code mandatory and took effect on 1 January 2010 - converting investigation from an undertaking into an obligation.

SOLAS regulation I/21 is the older and broader provision: each Administration undertakes to conduct an investigation of any casualty occurring to its ships subject to the Convention when it judges that the investigation may assist in identifying what changes to the Convention might be desirable.

MARPOL Article 12 - Casualties to ships: each Administration undertakes to investigate any casualty occurring to its ships subject to the Convention where the casualty has produced a major deleterious effect upon the marine environment, and to supply the Organization with information concerning the findings.

Behind both sits UNCLOS Article 94(7), requiring an inquiry into marine casualties on the high seas involving loss of life, serious injury to another State's nationals, or serious damage to ships, installations or the environment. The Code cites SOLAS I/21 and UNCLOS 94(7) together.

blocks.h: 2. (b) The purpose and structure of the Code

blocks.p: The Code - resolution MSC.255(84) - provides a common approach to marine safety investigations. Its defining principle, and the thing to state first, is that a marine safety investigation is conducted to prevent future casualties, not to apportion blame or determine liability. It is separate from, and must not be prejudiced by, any criminal, disciplinary or civil proceedings. It is arranged in three parts:

ul: Part I - General provisions (chapters 1 to 3): purpose, definitions and application.
Part II - Mandatory standards (from chapter 4): what a State Party must do.
Part III - Recommended practices (from chapter 15): what it should do.
An impartial Marine Safety Investigation Authority (chapter 4), properly resourced.

Notification (chapter 5) - ship name and flag, IMO number, nature, location, time and date, numbers seriously injured or killed, consequences to persons, property and environment, and any other ship involved.
A safety investigation into every very serious marine casualty (chapter 6.1), with the flag State responsible for ensuring it is conducted and completed (6.2).

Agreement between substantially interested States (chapter 7) - the flag State may agree that another State conducts the investigation, and participating in it discharges its obligations under the Code, SOLAS I/21 and UNCLOS 94(7).
Powers of investigation, parallel investigations and co-operation (chapters 8 to 10).
Independence (chapter 11) - the investigation shall not be subject to external direction.
Obtaining evidence from seafarers (chapter 12) - they are informed of the nature and basis of the investigation and may be legally represented.
Draft reports (chapter 13) circulated to substantially interested States for comment, normally within 30 days.

Reports (chapter 14) - the final report of every very serious marine casualty investigation is submitted to the Organization, and so is any other report containing information that may prevent future casualties.
Administrative responsibilities and principles of investigation (chapters 15 and 16), and guidance on investigating casualties and incidents.
Confidentiality of marine safety records - statements, communications, medical and private information, analyses and voyage data recorder information - so that people speak freely to investigators.
Protection for witnesses and involved parties, notification to parties involved, co-ordination, evidence collection, and the re-opening of an investigation where significant new evidence emerges.

blocks.p: The Code defines it at paragraph 2.22: "A very serious marine casualty means a marine casualty involving the total loss of the ship or a death or severe damage to the environment." Three limbs, any one of which is sufficient. Reading it needs the supporting definitions: a marine casualty (2.9) is an event, or sequence of events, resulting directly in connection with the operation of a ship in death or serious injury, loss of a person overboard, loss, presumed loss or abandonment of a ship, or material damage; a serious injury (2.18) is one causing incapacitation for more than 72 hours commencing within seven days of the injury; and severe damage to the environment (2.19) is damage which, as evaluated by the affected State or the flag State, produces a major deleterious effect upon the environment.

The classification matters because it triggers obligations: a safety investigation is mandatory for every very serious marine casualty, and the final report must go to IMO. Note also that the Code defines only this term - the related expression "serious marine casualty" appears nowhere in it and comes from IMO's separate reporting guidance.

Three printed limbs and, this time, a printed weighting: (a) is a citation question at 5, (b) is the bulk at 7, and (c) is a definition at 4. Limb (a) is answered in a few lines if you know the regulation numbers and lost entirely if you do not, so learn them; limb (c) is worth quoting almost verbatim. Note a real change from the January 2026 setting of this question: the command in limb (b) is now Illustrate, where January printed Briefly write. The instruction to be brief has gone and the limb is now the heaviest at 7 marks, so a bare list is no longer enough - group the Code's mandatory standards under headings and give a concrete instance or two, while still keeping it structured rather than discursive.

blocks.h: The one sentence that must appear

blocks.p: A marine safety investigation is conducted to prevent future casualties, not to apportion blame or determine liability. That is the Code's whole philosophy, and everything else follows from it - why investigations must be independent of external direction, why marine safety records are confidential, why witnesses are protected, and why the investigation is kept separate from criminal and civil proceedings. If an answer omits it, the examiner cannot tell whether the candidate understands the Code or has merely listed its chapters.

Three provisions, and they do different jobs. SOLAS XI-1/6 is the mandatory hook - it makes Parts I and II of the Code mandatory and took effect on 1 January 2010. SOLAS I/21 is the older, discretionary undertaking, where the Administration investigates when it judges the investigation may assist in identifying desirable changes to the Convention. MARPOL Article 12 is the pollution counterpart, and note its threshold - a major deleterious effect upon the marine environment. Citing only XI-1/6 answers half of limb (a), because the question expressly asks for SOLAS and MARPOL.

ul: Giving only the SOLAS provision when the question asks for SOLAS and MARPOL. MARPOL Article 12 is the one - an Article, not a regulation in an Annex.
Confusing "very serious marine casualty" with "serious marine casualty". Only the first is defined in the Code; the second comes from IMO's reporting guidance and is not in MSC.255(84) at all.
Writing that the purpose of an investigation is to find who was at fault. It is the opposite, and it is the single most important point in the question.
Getting the serious-injury definition loosely. It is incapacitation for more than 72 hours, commencing within seven days of the injury.
Treating the whole Code as mandatory. Parts I and II are mandatory through SOLAS XI-1/6; Part III is recommended practice, and the question asks about both.
Forgetting that the final report of every very serious marine casualty investigation goes to IMO.

blocks.p:
"A crew member died - is that a very serious marine casualty?" Yes. The three limbs are total loss of the ship, or a death, or severe damage to the environment - any one is sufficient, and a death alone qualifies.

"Who investigates if the ship is Indian-flagged but the casualty is in another State's waters?" The flag State is responsible, but chapter 7 allows agreement with another substantially interested State to conduct it, and participation in that investigation discharges the flag State's obligations under the Code, SOLAS I/21 and UNCLOS 94(7).

"Can the investigation report be used in court?" The Code makes safety records confidential and keeps the safety investigation separate from criminal, disciplinary and civil proceedings, precisely so that evidence is given freely. That separation is a design feature, not an oversight.

ul: Which regulation makes the Casualty Investigation Code mandatory, and from when? SOLAS regulation XI-1/6, adopted by MSC.257(84), effective 1 January 2010.
Define a very serious marine casualty. A marine casualty involving the total loss of the ship, or a death, or severe damage to the environment.

What is a substantially interested State? Broadly: the flag State, the coastal State, a State whose environment was severely or significantly damaged, one whose nationals died or were seriously injured, or one with a significant interest recognised by the investigating State.

What is the difference between a marine casualty and a marine incident? An incident endangers, or would endanger if not corrected, the ship, its occupants or the environment - but it stops short of the outcomes that make a casualty, and it excludes deliberate acts intended to cause harm.
What must the notification contain? Ship name and flag, IMO number, nature, location, time and date, numbers seriously injured or killed, consequences, and any other ship involved.
Where does the final report go? To the Organization, for every very serious marine casualty investigation.

blocks.p: WHY - WHO - WHAT - WHEN. Why: prevention, not blame. Who: an independent Marine Safety Investigation Authority, with the flag State responsible and substantially interested States able to take over. What: notify, investigate, take evidence, draft, circulate for 30 days, report to IMO. When: mandatory for every very serious marine casualty. For the definition itself: SHIP - LIFE - SEA - total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment.

One point is worth stating carefully. The Code defines only "very serious marine casualty"; a search of the full Code text returns no occurrence of the expression "serious marine casualty" standing alone. That term belongs to IMO's separate casualty-reporting guidance, which sits outside the Code and has been revised over time. This answer therefore gives the Code's definition and identifies the other term as coming from elsewhere, rather than presenting a graded scale as though the Code contained one. The Code has also been amended since its 2008 adoption; the material relied on here - purpose, structure, the chapter 6 investigation duty and the chapter 2 definitions - is the stable core, but a candidate citing a specific paragraph number in an oral should be ready to say which edition they are quoting.

questions.understand_first: A marine safety investigation is not a trial, and the Code exists to keep it from becoming one. It is built so that people will tell an investigator the truth without that truth being used against them - hence independence from external direction, confidentiality of the records, protection for witnesses, and separation from criminal and civil proceedings. Once that purpose is clear, the structure of the Code stops looking like a list of chapters and starts looking like the conditions that make honest evidence possible.

blocks.h: 1. (a) What the human element means in STCW

blocks.p: STCW refuses to treat competence as something time served automatically confers. It replaces experience with demonstrated competence, then addresses the conditions - fitness, rest, teamwork and company responsibility - under which competence can actually be exercised. The instrument is the STCW Convention and Code, 1978, as amended, most significantly by the Manila amendments of 2010, in force from 1 January 2012.

ul: The Part A tables of competence specify, for every function and level, the competence required, the knowledge, understanding and proficiency behind it, the methods for demonstrating it and the criteria for evaluating it - so assessment is against a published standard, not an examiner's impression.
Part A is mandatory; Part B is guidance - a distinction worth stating.

The Manila amendments added mandatory training in leadership and teamworking at operational level and leadership and managerial skill at management level - where engine-room and bridge resource management, situational awareness and workload management enter the Convention. It is the explicit recognition that technically competent individuals still fail as a team.
Regulation I/6 governs training and assessment, and regulation I/8 requires a quality standards system, so the training system itself is audited rather than assumed.
Regulation I/11 requires periodic revalidation, and chapter VI mandatory safety familiarisation and basic training before a seafarer is assigned duties.

blocks.h: 3. Fitness for duty - the physical human being

ul: Regulation VIII/1 requires each Administration, for the purpose of preventing fatigue, to establish and enforce rest periods for watchkeeping personnel and for those with designated safety, security and pollution-prevention duties in accordance with section A-VIII/1, and to require that watch systems are arranged so that efficiency is not impaired by fatigue.

The Manila-amended A-VIII/1 minimum rest is 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period. The daily rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which shall be at least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive periods of rest shall not exceed 14 hours.

Authorised exceptions are tightly conditioned: weekly rest may not fall below 70 hours in any 7-day period, exceptions from the 77-hour norm may not run for more than two consecutive weeks, and daily rest may then be divided into no more than three periods.
The Manila amendments also introduced alcohol limits for masters, officers and other seafarers with designated safety, security and environmental duties.
Regulation I/9 sets medical fitness standards, and regulation VIII/2 with section A-VIII/2 governs watchkeeping arrangements and principles.

blocks.h: 4. Responsibility placed on companies and Administrations

blocks.p: Regulation I/14 makes the company responsible for ensuring seafarers hold valid certificates, are familiarised with their duties and the ship's arrangements, and that documentation is maintained - so the human element is not left as an individual's problem. Administrations operate quality standards and are subject to independent evaluation and reporting to IMO.

blocks.h: 5. (b) The impact of fatigue on seafarer performance

blocks.p: The question asks for a critical examination, so state the effects and then say what follows from them. Fatigue is not tiredness; it is a measurable degradation of the capacities the job depends on. It reduces vigilance and sustained attention - precisely what a lookout and a duty engineer on an unmanned machinery space are there for. It lengthens reaction time and impairs judgement, decision-making and risk perception, so a fatigued officer is not merely slower but readier to accept a risk they would refuse when rested. It causes memory lapses, loss of situational awareness, and microsleeps - intrusions of sleep lasting seconds of which the person has no awareness, which is why self-assessment of fitness is unreliable.

ul: Sleep debt is cumulative - short sleep across successive days accrues a deficit one long sleep does not repay, so performance can be degraded on a day when last night's rest looks adequate on paper.
Circadian timing matters as much as duration - the alertness trough falls in the small hours, coinciding with the 0000-0400 watch, and rest against the body clock is of lower quality hour for hour.
The marine environment adds its own loading - motion, noise, vibration, heat, split rest, port workload, inspections and short-sea schedules.
It causes casualties. Fatigue is a recognised contributory factor in groundings, collisions and personal injury, and one investigators look for under the Casualty Investigation Code.

The critical point, and where the marks are: the regulatory instrument is a prescriptive hours-of-rest formula, and compliance with it is not the same as being rested. A schedule can satisfy 10 in 24 and 77 in 7 and still leave an officer impaired, because it says nothing about circadian timing, sleep quality, accumulated debt or workload. Closing that gap is what company fatigue management is for.

blocks.h: 6. (b) IMO measures, and what a shipping company can implement

blocks.p: What the IMO has done. The principal instrument is the Guidelines on fatigue, MSC.1/Circ.1598, approved at MSC 100 and issued on 24 January 2019, superseding MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001. It is recommendatory, and it is deliberately addressed to everyone who can affect the outcome, in six modules - fatigue and its causes; the Company; the seafarer; awareness and training; ship design; and Administrations and port State authorities. Behind it sit the mandatory provisions: STCW regulation VIII/1 with Code section A-VIII/1, requiring minimum rest of 10 hours in any 24 and 77 hours in any 7 days, taken in no more than two periods of which one is at least 6 hours, with no more than 14 hours between them; and MLC 2006 Regulations 2.3, 2.4 and 2.7 on hours of work and rest, leave and manning. The IMO has also worked the human element through the ISM Code, which requires the company to ensure the ship is appropriately manned.

ul: Man the ship for the work, not for the minimum. The single most effective company measure. A manning level and a voyage plan that only work if everyone runs at their maximum permitted hours has no margin for a port call, a breakdown or an inspection.

Put a fatigue policy in the safety management system under the ISM Code, with the Company's responsibility and the master's authority stated, so fatigue is a managed hazard rather than an individual weakness.

Schedule against the body clock. Where the trade allows, plan demanding work outside the circadian low, avoid abrupt watch rotation, and protect a consolidated sleep period rather than fragmenting rest.

Manage the port and inspection load - the point at which rest hours are actually lost. Plan surveys, bunkering and PSC inspections so that the same officers are not carrying them on top of a full watch cycle.

Audit the rest records honestly. Records that are always exactly compliant should be treated as a warning rather than a reassurance; the company should compare recorded rest with the actual work programme.
Provide reporting without blame. A seafarer must be able to report that they are unfit to keep a watch without it counting against them, or the policy is decorative.
Train for it. Awareness of sleep debt, circadian effects, microsleeps and the unreliability of self-assessment, for masters, officers and ratings alike.

Design and maintain for rest - noise and vibration in accommodation, blackout, temperature control and alarm management, which is where a chief engineer's decisions bear directly on whether off-watch rest is restorative.

blocks.p: Two printed limbs of 8 marks each, so split the answer evenly and head each limb clearly. Limb A rewards structure - competence tables, fitness for duty, company responsibility - and limb B rewards naming the actual circular. A candidate who writes generally about tiredness for the second limb without producing MSC.1/Circ.1598 and its module structure will lose most of eight marks, because "the IMO guidance" is a specific document.

blocks.h: The organising idea for limb A

blocks.p: STCW attacks the human element on three fronts, and saying so gives the limb a spine: can they do it (competence standards, assessed against published criteria), are they fit to do it now (fitness for duty - rest, medical, alcohol), and who is responsible for making that possible (regulation I/14, the company). The Manila amendments strengthened all three, and added the fourth dimension the older Convention lacked - can they work as a team, through mandatory leadership and teamworking training.

blocks.h: The numbers you must get right

blocks.p: 10 hours in any 24, and 77 hours in any 7 days. Divided into no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours, with no more than 14 hours between consecutive rest periods. Exceptions may not go below 70 hours in any 7 days and may not run more than two consecutive weeks. Learn 10, 77, 2, 6, 14, 70 - and be careful, because 70 and 77 are both real figures doing different jobs: 77 is the norm, 70 is the floor under an authorised exception. Quoting 70 as the normal requirement is the classic error, and it is exactly the trap that a pre-2010 copy of the Code will lead you into.

blocks.h: Currency - what applies and what does not

blocks.p: The operative regime is STCW 1978 as amended, with the Manila amendments in force from 1 January 2012. A comprehensive review of the STCW Convention and Code has been under way through the HTW Sub-Committee with completion targeted around 2027 - one of the acknowledged gaps being the treatment of hours of rest. Nothing had been adopted at the date of this paper, and nothing had been adopted when this answer was written. So write the Manila regime as current, and mention the review only as work in progress. Do not present any reviewed text as though it were in force.

ul: Answering limb B without naming MSC.1/Circ.1598 and the circular it replaced, MSC/Circ.1014.
Treating the fatigue Guidelines as mandatory. They are recommendatory; the binding requirements are STCW chapter VIII and MLC 2006.
Quoting 70 hours as the normal weekly rest. 77 is the norm; 70 is the minimum where an exception has been authorised.
Confusing hours of rest with hours of work. MLC permits either a maximum-hours-of-work or a minimum-hours-of-rest approach; STCW A-VIII/1 is expressed as minimum rest.

Writing about STCW competence generally without mentioning that the Manila amendments made leadership and teamworking training mandatory - that is the human-element addition the question is really pointing at.
Forgetting regulation I/14. The human element is not only about the seafarer; the company carries defined obligations.

blocks.p:
"Your rest-hour records show full compliance. Is your crew rested?" Not necessarily, and the Guidelines say so - the formula is prescriptive, and quality of rest depends on circadian rhythm and accumulated sleep debt. Records that are always exactly compliant deserve suspicion, not comfort.

"Is coffee a fatigue countermeasure?" The Guidelines address it directly: caffeine can improve alertness temporarily but is not a substitute for adequate sleep and rest, and can interfere with sleep afterwards.

"Where do the fatigue Guidelines actually bite on board?" Through the safety management system - Module 2 is addressed to the company, so fatigue risk belongs in manning, scheduling and the ISM Code procedures rather than being left to individual willpower.

ul: Which circular contains the IMO fatigue Guidelines? MSC.1/Circ.1598 of 24 January 2019, approved at MSC 100, replacing MSC/Circ.1014.
How many modules, and who are they addressed to? Six - fatigue itself, the company, the seafarer, awareness and training, ship design, and the Administration and port State authorities.
State the minimum hours of rest. 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 in any 7-day period; no more than two periods, one at least 6 hours; intervals not exceeding 14 hours.
When do the Manila amendments date from? Adopted 2010, in force 1 January 2012.
Which STCW regulation makes the company responsible? Regulation I/14 - valid certificates, familiarisation and documentation.
Are the fatigue Guidelines mandatory? No. STCW chapter VIII and MLC 2006 carry the mandatory requirements; the Guidelines are recommendatory.

Limb B by audience: WHAT IT IS - COMPANY - SEAFARER - TRAINING - SHIP - REGULATOR, which is the six modules in order. The numbers: 10 / 77 / 2 / 6 / 14, floor 70.

blocks.p: The fatigue limb is primary-verified: the circular number, date, approving session, the superseded circular and the six module titles were all read in the text of MSC.1/Circ.1598, as were the sleep-debt definition and the statement about the prescriptive STCW formula. The rest-hour figures carry a caveat worth recording. MIW holds no licensed copy of the STCW Convention and Code. An IMO circular copy of section A-VIII/1 was consulted first and turned out to be the pre-Manila 1995 text - five paragraphs, 70 hours per seven-day period, and no 14-hour interval rule. Taking it at face value would have produced a confidently wrong answer. The Manila-amended figures used here therefore come from a competent-authority notice reproducing the amended regime, which also confirms the 1 January 2012 entry into force. They are consistent across sources and are safe to use, but they sit at authoritative-secondary status rather than primary, and acquiring a licensed STCW Code would promote them. The lesson generalises: for an amended instrument, confirm which edition a source is reproducing before quoting a number from it.

questions.understand_first: The human element is not a soft topic bolted onto a technical convention. STCW treats it as three separate engineering problems: whether a person has a demonstrated capability, whether they are in a fit state to use it right now, and whose job it is to make that possible. Fatigue is the clearest case of the second problem, which is why it gets both a hard rule - a rest-hour formula you can audit - and a soft one, a set of Guidelines admitting that a compliant record does not prove a rested watchkeeper.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the weekly minimum rest 70 or 77 hours?

retrieval_cards.why: They are organised by audience, which makes them easy to recall.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are the fatigue Guidelines mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: No - they are recommendatory. The mandatory requirements are the rest-hour provisions of STCW chapter VIII and the corresponding MLC 2006 requirements.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What did the Manila amendments add that speaks directly to the human element?
retrieval_cards.answer: Mandatory training in leadership and teamworking at operational level and leadership and managerial skill at management level - which is how engine-room and bridge resource management, situational awareness and workload management entered the Convention. Alcohol limits were also introduced.
retrieval_cards.why: Technically competent individuals can still fail as a team.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do the Guidelines define sleep debt?
retrieval_cards.answer: Insufficient accumulated sleep over multiple consecutive 24-hour periods. It reduces alertness and performance, and in the long term affects health.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why a formally compliant rest record can still leave a watchkeeper impaired.

retrieval_cards.answer: Not necessarily. The Guidelines note that the STCW formula is prescriptive and that circadian rhythm and sleep debt determine rest quality, and that rest means rest rather than substituting a different form of work.
retrieval_cards.why: Records that are always exactly compliant deserve suspicion, not comfort.
